explanations.explanation: Night it is. Nehemiah says, “I set out at night with a few men.” (Nehemiah 2:12) He inspects the wall by night again when he goes up the valley (Nehemiah 2:15). Friend, I've sat in the dark for years, and I still wouldn't pick a wall tour for it.

Sunrise is a lovely time for a walk, but it isn't the one here. Nehemiah says, “I set out at night with a few men.” (Nehemiah 2:12) The sun doesn't come up anywhere in that verse. I think a sunrise tour would have had a lot more eyes on it, but that's my guess, not the text's.

Midday, with the sun straight overhead, is a different story entirely. Nehemiah says, “I set out at night with a few men.” (Nehemiah 2:12) He's inspecting by night again in verse 15 (Nehemiah 2:15). Noon is when my ovens already have me sweating, so I'm glad nobody asked me to walk walls then.

Not a soul. Nehemiah says, “I did not tell anyone what my God had laid on my heart to do for Jerusalem.” (Nehemiah 2:12) Verse 16 adds that the officials didn't know where he had gone or what he was doing (Nehemiah 2:16). That's a man holding a secret tighter than a lid on a cookie jar.

The priests are actually on the list of people he hadn't told. Nehemiah says, “I had not yet told the Jews or priests or nobles or officials or any other workers.” (Nehemiah 2:16) So the priests are in the same boat as everybody else. Nobody got a special heads-up.

The nobles didn't get a private preview either. Nehemiah says, “I had not yet told the Jews or priests or nobles or officials or any other workers.” (Nehemiah 2:16) There they are, right in the middle of that list. A secret that stays secret from the nobles is a REAL secret.

Gates it is. Nehemiah inspects “the walls of Jerusalem that had been broken down and the gates that had been destroyed by fire.” (Nehemiah 2:13) Broken walls AND burned gates, that's a double dose of rough. He names the gates again when he speaks to the people: “its gates have been burned down.” (Nehemiah 2:17)

Towers do show up in chapter 3, like the Tower of the Hundred (Nehemiah 3:1), but not in this verse. Here the text says Nehemiah inspected “the gates that had been destroyed by fire.” (Nehemiah 2:13) So the fire is tied to the gates in this line. The towers just wandered into the wrong verse.

No houses on this tour, friend. Verse 13 says he inspected the walls that had been broken down and the gates that had been destroyed by fire (Nehemiah 2:13). This is a wall and gate inspection, not an open house with a clipboard.

The animal it is. Nehemiah says, “there was no room for the animal under me to get through.” (Nehemiah 2:14) Back in verse 12 he told us the only animal with him was the one he was riding (Nehemiah 2:12). So it's one rider, one animal, and one gap that's too tight.

The text puts the squeeze on the animal, not the men. Nehemiah says, “there was no room for the animal under me to get through.” (Nehemiah 2:14) Nothing says the men with him were stuck. Only the animal had a problem with that gap.

There's no cart anywhere in this story. Nehemiah says the only animal with him was the one he was riding (Nehemiah 2:12), and that's what couldn't get through (Nehemiah 2:14). Just a rider and his ride. A cart would have added a whole parking problem on top of it.

Together is the word. Nehemiah says, “Come, let us rebuild the wall of Jerusalem, so that we will no longer be a disgrace.” (Nehemiah 2:17) He doesn't point at everybody else and walk off. He says “us” and puts himself right inside it.

Nobody's packing a moving truck in this verse. Nehemiah says, “Come, let us rebuild the wall of Jerusalem, so that we will no longer be a disgrace.” (Nehemiah 2:17) The plan is to stay and fix the place they're standing in. Moving would be the exact opposite direction.

explanations.answer: Ask the king to send builders
explanations.explanation: The king does come up, but the plan is a different one. Nehemiah tells the people what the king had said (Nehemiah 2:18). What he asks of them, though, is “Come, let us rebuild the wall of Jerusalem…” (Nehemiah 2:17). The call is for "us" to do the rebuilding.

True, and he says it plainly. “Come, let us rebuild the wall of Jerusalem, so that we will no longer be a disgrace.” (Nehemiah 2:17) No sprinkles on that one, just plain dough. The wall is the plan, and not being a disgrace is what he names as the reason.

That one is true after all. Nehemiah says, “Come, let us rebuild the wall of Jerusalem, so that we will no longer be a disgrace.” (Nehemiah 2:17) That "so that" ties the wall straight to no longer being a disgrace. And he says "we," so he's counting himself in with everybody else.

Nobody asks for time to think here. The people reply, “Let us start rebuilding,” and then they set their hands to this good work. (Nehemiah 2:18) That's a quick yes with hands attached. I've seen folks take longer to pick a cookie flavor.

False is the answer, because the people don't ask for any time at all. They reply, “Let us start rebuilding,” and then they set their hands to this good work. (Nehemiah 2:18) No "let me check my calendar," no group chat debate. Just a yes and then hands going to work.

Mocking and ridiculing is what the text says. When Sanballat, Tobiah and Geshem heard about it, they “mocked us and ridiculed us.” (Nehemiah 2:19) Then they asked, “What is this you are doing?” They showed up with questions instead of trowels.

explanations.answer: Offer to help with the wall
explanations.explanation: These three don't come offering help. Nehemiah says they “mocked us and ridiculed us.” (Nehemiah 2:19) Nobody's showing up with a ladder in this verse. They show up with comments.

In these verses, they use words. Nehemiah says they “mocked us and ridiculed us,” and they ask if the builders are rebelling against the king (Nehemiah 2:19). There's no attack and no night raid in what the text tells us here. Words only, so hold your horses, friend.

Rebelling is the word. They ask, “Are you rebelling against the king?” (Nehemiah 2:19) That's quite a charge to throw at people who just agreed to fix a wall. And Nehemiah had already told those people what the king had said (Nehemiah 2:18).

Complaining is what I do when I find a burnt batch, but it's not the word here. The three ask, “Are you rebelling against the king?” (Nehemiah 2:19) Their question is about the king and a rebellion. Nobody's grumbling in that line.

They don't say sinning. Sanballat, Tobiah and Geshem ask, “Are you rebelling against the king?” (Nehemiah 2:19) Their word is rebelling, and it's all about the king. It's a big accusation, and it's not the one in the blank.

The God of heaven. Nehemiah answers them, “The God of heaven is the One who will grant us success.” (Nehemiah 2:20) Then he adds, “We, His servants, will start rebuilding…” (Nehemiah 2:20). So God grants the success, and the servants start building.

The king matters in this story, since Nehemiah told his people what the king had said (Nehemiah 2:18). But when the mockers push back, Nehemiah says, “The God of heaven is the One who will grant us success.” (Nehemiah 2:20) So when it comes to who grants success, Nehemiah names God, not the king.

The people do the building, no question. Nehemiah says, “We, His servants, will start rebuilding…” (Nehemiah 2:20). But the One who grants success, he says, is “The God of heaven.” (Nehemiah 2:20) The builders bring the work, and the success comes from Him.

Nehemiah says the opposite. He tells the three, “you have no portion, right, or claim in Jerusalem.” (Nehemiah 2:20) That's three words in a row, portion, right and claim, and he says none to every one of them.

False is the answer, and Nehemiah is firm about it. He tells Sanballat, Tobiah and Geshem, “you have no portion, right, or claim in Jerusalem.” (Nehemiah 2:20) Portion, right, claim, he hands them the whole list with a big no on each one. That's a no-refunds kind of answer.
